Meccan. It has ninety-six letters, twenty words, and five verses.

Naqil ibn Raqim informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Shadhah narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Salim ibn Qutaybah narrated to us, from Shu'bah, from 'Asim, from Zirr, from Ubayy, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Fil, God, Mighty and Majestic, will protect him during the days of his life in this world from slander and transformation."

[259] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 10/441.]]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾

The story, and with God is success.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: The account of the companions of the elephant, as related by some scholars, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from others among the scholars of Yemen and elsewhere who met them, is that a king of the Himyar called Zar'ah Dhu Nuwas had become a Jew, and the Himyar united with him in this, except the people of Najran, who were Christians according to the original ruling of the Gospel (Injil). They had a leader called 'Abd Allah ibn al-Tamir. He invited them to Judaism, but they refused, so he gave them a choice, and they chose death. He dug a trench for them and devised for them various kinds of execution.

Some of them were killed by being made to stand as targets, and others he burned in the fire of the trench. But a man from Saba' called Dawas ibn Tha'laban escaped on his horse and galloped until he outran them in the sand. He went to Caesar (Qayṣar) and told him what had befallen them and asked for help. Caesar said: "Your land is far from us, but I will write to the king of Abyssinia, for he is on our religion, and he will support you." So he wrote to the Negus (al-Najashi), ordering him to support him.

When he came to the Negus, the Negus sent with him a man from Abyssinia called Aryat. When he sent him off, he said: "If you enter Yemen, kill a third of its men, destroy a third of its land, and send me a third of its captives." When he entered it, he encountered some resistance in battle, and they scattered away from Dhu Nuwas, and his horse carried him off into the sea, where it struck him, and both of them perished together. That was the last of him. Aryat entered Yemen and acted according to what the Negus had ordered.

Dhu Hadr al-Himyari said, concerning what befell the people of Yemen and their soil:

"My eye, may you have no father, you could not bear it; may God save you, for my spittle has run dry,
At the sound of the singing girls when we were intoxicated, and when we were given to drink the choicest wine,
And drinking wine is no shame for me, if my companion does not reproach me for it,
And Ghumdan, of which I told you, whose sons held it aloft on a cliff's summit,
Its lamps of olive oil shining within it, like the flashes of lightning when it is evening,
Then it became ashes after its splendor, and the flame of fire changed its beauty,
And Dhu Nuwas submitted, having given his all, and warned his people of the narrowness of the strait."

[[The verses in full are in Tafsir al-Tabari: 1/547.]]

He said: Aryat remained in Yemen, and the Negus wrote to him: "Hold your position with your army and those with you." He remained for a time. Then Abraha ibn al-Sabah became angry over a matter concerning Abyssinia, until they split into two factions: one group was with him, and another group was with Abraha. Then they clashed. When some of them drew close to others, Abraha sent to Aryat: "Do not let the Abyssinians fight one another in any way until you meet me. Instead, come out to me, and whichever of us kills the other, the army will join him." So he sent to him: "You have been fair."

Aryat was a large, tall, and handsome man, with his spear in his hand. Abraha was a short man, cautious and fleshy, and he had been devout in Christianity. He had left behind a young man (ghulam) called 'Utudah. When they drew near, Aryat raised his spear and struck Abraha's head with it. It fell upon his forehead, splitting his eye, forehead, nose, and lip, and for this reason he was called al-Ashram (the one with the split nose).

'Utudah charged at Aryat and killed him. The Abyssinians gathered around Abraha, and 'Utudah said: "I am 'Utudah, from behind him. I will strike him, neither father nor mother could match his blow." Abraha said: "There was nothing for you before him, O 'Utudah, nor will there be blood money for him." The Negus heard of what Abraha had done, became angry, and swore that he would not leave Abraha until he dragged him by his forelock and trampled his land. He wrote to Abraha: "You have transgressed against my governor and killed him without my command."

Abraha was an arrogant man. When he heard what the Negus had said, he shaved his head, filled a sack with soil from his land, and wrote to the Negus: "O King, Aryat was only your slave, and I am your slave. We disagreed about your affair, and you know Abyssinia better and govern it better. I had wanted him to withdraw and for me to govern it, but he refused, so I killed him. I have heard what the king swore, and I have shaved my head and sent it to him, and I have sent him a sack of soil from his land so that he may place it under his feet." When that reached him, he was pleased with him and confirmed him in his post, and wrote to him to remain with those of the army who were with him.

Then Abraha built a church in Sana'a called al-Qulays, and he wrote to the Negus: "I have built for you in Sana'a a church the like of which no king has ever built, and I will not stop until I divert to it the pilgrimage of the Arabs." A man from the Banu Malik ibn Kinanah heard of this, so he went out to al-Qulays, entered it at night, and sat there. It was reported to Abraha, and it is said that he came to it looking at it, and Abraha entered and found the filth (al-'adhirah). He said: "Who has dared against me?" It was said: "A man from the Arabs, from the people of that House, did this. He heard what you said and did this." Abraha swore at that moment that he would march to the Ka'bah until he destroyed it.

He set out marching with the Abyssinians, and with him he brought the elephant. The Arabs heard of this, and they were greatly alarmed and found it hideous, and they regarded fighting him as a duty upon them. A king of the Himyar called Dhu Nafar came out with those of his people who obeyed him, and he confronted Abraha, defeated him, and captured Dhu Nafar, bringing him to Abraha. Dhu Nafar said: "O King, do not kill me, for sparing me is better for you than killing me." So he spared him and bound him.

Abraha was a forbearing man. Then he set out marching until he approached the lands of Khath'am. Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami came out with the two tribes of Khath'am, Shahran and Nahs, and those who had gathered to him from the tribes of Yemen. They fought him, and he defeated them and captured Nufayl. Nufayl said: "O King, I am a guide in the land of the Arabs. Do not kill me, and these two hands of mine are pledged for my people to hear and obey." So he spared him and took him along to guide him. When he passed by al-Ta'if, Mas'ud ibn Mu'attib came out to him with men of Thaqif and said: "O King, we are only your slaves, and we have no opposition to you. This house of ours is not the house you seek"—meaning al-Lat—"you seek only the House in Mecca. We will send someone to guide you to it." They sent Abu Righal, their client (mawla), and he went until, when he reached al-Mughammas, Abu Righal died. He is the one whose grave is stoned.

From al-Mughammas, Abraha sent a man from the Habash called al-Aswad ibn Maqsud at the head of his cavalry vanguard. He gathered the wealth of the Sanctuary (haram) and seized two hundred camels belonging to 'Abd al-Muttalib. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar ibn Makhzum said:

"O God, disgrace al-Aswad ibn Maqsud,
the one who seized the large herd, with the marked camels among them,
Between Hira' and Thabir and the desert, detaining them while they are following one after another,
Gather them to the black Tamatim [[the non-Arab foreigners]], who have agreed, or may there be a deity to be worshipped,
And they demolish the sacred House, the honored one, and the two hills of Safa and Marwah and the sacred sites,
Dash him, O Lord, and You are the Praised."

[[Al-hajmah: a large herd of camels. Al-taqlid: marking an animal as an offering. Al-bayd: plural of bayda', a wilderness. Hira' and Thabir: two mountains in Mecca. Tatrid of camels: their following one after another. Al-tamatim: the foreigners.]]

Then Abraha sent Hanatah al-Himyari to the people of Mecca and said: "Ask about its chief, then convey to him what I have sent you with. Tell him that I did not come to fight, but only to demolish this House." He went and entered Mecca, and met 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim and said: "The king has sent me to you to tell you that he has not come to fight unless you fight him, but he has come only to demolish this House, and then he will depart from you."

'Abd al-Muttalib said: "We have no power against him, nor do we have the means to confront him. We will leave him free to do what he came for, for this is the Sacred House of God and the House of His friend Abraham (peace be upon him). If He protects it, it is His House and His sanctuary; and if He leaves it between him and that, by God, we have no strength against it." He said: "Come with me to the king." It is claimed by some scholars that he rode with him on a mule that he had and some of his sons rode with him, until they reached the army.

Dhu Nafar was a friend of 'Abd al-Muttalib, so he came to him and said: "O Dhu Nafar, do you have any help to offer in what has befallen us?"

He said: "What help can a captive man give who cannot be sure he will not be killed morning and evening? But I will send to Unays, the elephant driver, for he is a friend of mine. Ask him to do for you what good he can before the king, and to exalt your rank and standing with him."

He sent for Unays, who came to him, and he said: "This is the chief of Quraysh and the owner of the caravans of Mecca, who feeds people in the plains and the wilderness and on the mountain peaks. The king has seized two hundred camels from him. If you can help him with the king, then do so, for he is my friend, and I love that he should receive whatever good may reach him." Unays entered upon Abraha and said: "O King, this is the chief of Quraysh and the owner of the caravans of Mecca, who feeds people in the plains and the wilderness and on the mountain peaks. He asks permission to see you, and I would like you to permit him so that he may speak with you. He has come not opposing you nor hostile to you, so grant him permission."

'Abd al-Muttalib was a large, tall, and handsome man. When Abraha saw him, he was impressed and honored him, but he disliked that he should sit with him on his throne and that he should sit beneath him. So he came down to the carpet and sat upon it, then he called him and had him sit with him. Then he said to his interpreter: "Tell him: what is your need of the king?" The interpreter said that to him.

'Abd al-Muttalib said: "My need of the king is that he return to me the two hundred camels he has taken from me." Abraha said to his interpreter: "You impressed me when I saw you, but now I have lost respect for you." He said: "Why?" He said: "You came to a House which is your religion and the religion of your fathers, and your protection, to demolish it, and you did not speak to me about it, but you speak to me about two hundred camels that were taken from you?" 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "I am the lord of these camels, and this House has a Lord who will protect it."

He said: "He will not prevent me from it." He said: "Then you and that matter." So he ordered his camels returned to him.

Ibn Ishaq said: It is claimed by some scholars that he went to Abraha with 'Umar ibn Nathah [[So it is in the manuscript; perhaps it is: Layth.]] ibn 'Adi ibn al-Wa'il ibn Bakr ibn 'Abd Manat ibn Kinanah, who at that time was the chief of the Banu Kinanah, and Khuwaylid ibn Wa'ilah al-Hudhali, who at that time was the chief of the Banu Hudhayl. They offered Abraha a third of the wealth of the people of Tihamah on condition that he would turn back from them and not demolish the House, but he refused. When the camels were returned to 'Abd al-Muttalib, he went out and informed Quraysh of the news, and told them to disperse into the ravines and take refuge on the mountain peaks, fearing for them the harm of the army when it entered. They did so. 'Abd al-Muttalib came to the Ka'bah, took hold of the ring of the door, and began to say:

"O Lord, I hope for none but You for them,
O Lord, protect from them Your sanctuary.
Let not their cross or their stratagems overcome Your devotees tomorrow.
They have brought the armies of their lands and the elephant to take Your dependents captive.
They have aimed at Your sanctuary with their scheming, in ignorance, and they have not regarded Your majesty.
If You are leaving them and our Ka'bah, then do as You see fit."

[[Zad al-Masir: 8/310, and Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/554.]]

Then 'Abd al-Muttalib left the ring and went off with his people in some of those directions. Abraha awoke at al-Mughammas, prepared for entry, arranged his army, and readied his elephant. The name of the elephant was Mahmud. It was the elephant of the Negus, which he had sent to Abraha, and it was an elephant the like of which had not been seen on earth in size, body, and strength.

It is said that there were twelve elephants with him. Nufayl came to the largest elephant, took hold of its ear, and said: "Kneel, Mahmud, and return safely from where you came, for you are in the sacred land of God." The elephant knelt, and they tried to make it rise, but it refused. They struck it on the head with the iron hook, but it refused. They put their hooks beneath its belly and its elbows and pulled it to make it stand, but it refused. They turned it back toward Yemen, and it got up and ran; they turned it toward Syria, and it did the same; they turned it toward the east, and it did the same. Then they turned it toward the Sanctuary, and it knelt and refused to rise. It ran off, galloping, until it climbed the mountain.

God sent birds from the sea, like swallows (khatatif), each bird carrying three stones: two stones in its feet, and a stone in its beak, like chickpeas and lentils. When they came over them, it released them upon them, and those stones struck no one without him perishing.

Not all of the people were struck, and they went out fleeing, rushing along the road by which they had come, asking about Nufayl ibn Habib to guide them to the road to Yemen. Nufayl ibn Habib said, when he saw what God had brought down upon them of His vengeance:

"Where is the escape, when the God is the one who seeks?
And the Ashram, the defeated, not the victor?"

[[al-Ashram: he is Abraha, so called because a stone struck him and split his nose.]] [[Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/555.]]

Nufayl also said about that:

"Did not greet us, O Radinah? Yes, you have greeted us, and we have given you our eye with the dawn.
Radinah, if you had seen and had not been seen by the side of al-Muhassab, we would have seen what we saw,
Then you would have excused me, and praised my opinion, and you would not have grieved over what had passed between us.
I praised God when I saw the birds, and I feared stones that would fall upon us.
So all the people ask about Nufayl, as if I owed a debt to the Abyssinians."

[[The same source: 1/555, Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 20/199, and al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah: 2/216.]]

Nufayl was watching them from some of the mountains, while the people were crying out and some were agitating against others. They went out falling along every road and dying at every watering place. A disease fell upon Abraha's body, and his fingertips began to fall off. Every time a fingertip fell, a stream of pus and blood followed it. He reached Sana'a like a young bird, with those of his companions who remained, and he did not die until his chest split open from his heart, and then he perished.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman claimed that the cause that led to the story of the companions of the elephant was that a group from Quraysh went out as merchants to the land of the Negus. They traveled until they approached the seashore, and in one of its sand dunes there was a church of the Christians, which Quraysh called the Haykal, and the Negus and the people of his land called it Atas Hanan. The people knelt to block it, gathered firewood, and lit a fire and cooked. When they departed, they left the fire as it was on a windy day. The winds rushed, and the Haykal burst into flames. The messenger went to the Negus and informed him. At that, he was grieved with anger for the church, so Abraha was sent to demolish the Ka'bah [and what he encountered].

In Mecca at that time was Abu Mas'ud al-Thaqafi, who was blind. He spent summers in al-Ta'if and winters in Mecca. He was an intelligent and noble man who decided matters by his opinion, and he was the first to mend and the first to sever. He was a close friend of 'Abd al-Muttalib. 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "O Abu Mas'ud, what do you have to offer? This is a day in which one cannot do without your opinion."

Abu Mas'ud said to 'Abd al-Muttalib: "Go to a hundred camels and make them a sacred offering to God, mark them with sandals, and then station them in the Sanctuary. Perhaps some of these blacks will slaughter some of them, and the Lord of this House will be angered and seize them." 'Abd al-Muttalib did so. The people went to those camels, attacked them, and slaughtered some of them, and 'Abd al-Muttalib began to supplicate.

Abu Mas'ud said: [and 'Abd al-Muttalib said]: "This House has a Lord who protects it. Tubba', the king of Yemen, came to this rock of the House and wished to demolish it, but God prevented him and afflicted him, and darkness fell upon him for three days. When Tubba' saw that, he clothed the House in white Coptic cloth, honored it, and slaughtered sacrificial camels for it. So look toward the House."

'Abd al-Muttalib looked and said: "I see white birds rising from the seashore." He said: "Watch them with your eyes, and see where they settle." He said: "I see that they have gathered over our heads." He said: "Do you know them?" He said: "By God, I do not know them. They are neither from Najd, nor from Tihamah, nor Arab, nor Syrian, and they are birds in our land that are not familiar."

He said: "What is their shape?" He said: "They are like swallows, with pebbles in their beaks like pebbles of Hadhdh, and they came like locusts, pushing one another, in front of every bird, led by one with a red beak, black head, and long neck. They came until, when they were opposite the army, they settled over their heads."

When all the flocks had gathered, the birds poured what was in their beaks over those beneath them. Written upon each stone was the name of its owner. Then they turned back from where they had come. When morning came, the two of them descended from the peak of the mountain and walked slowly, and they did not see anyone; then they drew near, walking slowly, and heard no sound. They said: "The people spent the night in a stupor and have awakened asleep." When they drew near the army, behold, they were all dead.

A stone would fall upon one of their eggs (or heads), piercing it until it reached the brain, and would pierce the elephant and the animal, and the stone would sink into the earth from the force of its impact. 'Abd al-Muttalib then took one of their axes and dug until he reached deep into the earth, and filled it with red gold and fine jewels. He dug for his companion and filled it, and then said to Abu Mas'ud: "Bring your ring and choose. If you want, you may take my pit, if you want, you may take yours, and if you want, both of them are yours together."

Then Ibn Mas'ud said: "You chose me over yourself." 'Abd al-Muttalib replied: "I have not failed to place the finest of goods in my pit, so it is yours." Each of them sat by his pit, and 'Abd al-Muttalib called out to the people, so they returned and took from their surplus until they could no longer bear it. 'Abd al-Muttalib thereby became the leader of Quraysh, and they granted him the leadership. 'Abd al-Muttalib and Abu Mas'ud remained, with their families, in wealth from that money. God repelled [the enemy] from His Ka'bah and His qiblah, sending against them hosts they had no power to withstand.

Al-Waqidi said, with his chains of narration: Abraha sent Aryat, Abu Dukhma, with four thousand [men] to Yemen. He overcame it, honored the kings and humiliated the poor. Then a man from Abyssinia called Abraha al-Ashram, Abu Yaksum, rose up and called for obedience to himself, and they answered him. He killed Aryat and overcame Yemen. He saw people preparing for the Hajj and said: "Where are the people going?" He was told: "They are making pilgrimage to the House of God in Makkah." He said: "What is it made of?" He was told: "Of stones." He said: "What is its covering?" He was told: "What comes from here and there."

He said: "By the Messiah, I will build for them something better than it." So he built for them a house, constructed of white, red, yellow and black marble, adorned it with gold and silver, surrounded it with jewels, placed in it a great red ruby, appointed chamberlains for it, burned aloes wood (al-mandali) in it, and smeared its walls with musk, so that they blackened, until the jewels were hidden. He ordered the people to make pilgrimage to it, and many tribes of the Arabs made pilgrimage to it for years. Men remained in it worshipping and devoting themselves to it, and they performed rites for it.

Nufayl al-Khath'ami used to annoy him with what he disliked, so he was given respite. Then one night he saw no one moving, so he went, brought excrement, smeared it on its forehead, gathered carrion and threw it into it. Abraha was informed of this and became extremely angry, and said: "The Arabs have only acted out of zeal for their house. I will surely demolish it stone by stone." He wrote to the Negus informing him of this and asking him to send him his elephant Mahmud, an elephant unmatched on earth in size, body and strength, and he sent it to him.

When the elephant reached him, Abraha marched with the people, accompanied by the king of Himyar and Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami. When he approached the sacred precinct (al-haram), he ordered his companions to raid the people's camels, and they seized camels belonging to 'Abd al-Muttalib. Nufayl was a friend of 'Abd al-Muttalib, so he spoke to Abraha about his camels. Nufayl spoke to Abraha, saying: "O King, the chief of the Arabs, the most excellent of them in rank and the most ancient in nobility, has come to you; he carries [people] on thoroughbred horses, gives wealth, and feeds the people." So he was brought in to Abraha, who said: "What is your need?" He said: "That you return my camels to me." Abraha said: "I did not think, from what has reached me of you, except [that you would be] deceptive; I had thought you would speak to me about your House, which is your honor." 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "Return my camels to me, and as for the House, it has a Lord who will protect it."

So he ordered his camels returned to him. When he took them, he hung sandals on them, marked them, made them offerings, and let them loose in the sacred precinct so that some of them would be struck, and the Lord of the sacred precinct would be angered. 'Abd al-Muttalib went out on horses, accompanied by 'Amr ibn 'Abid ibn 'Imran ibn Makhzum ibn Mut'im ibn 'Adi, and Abu Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "O God, a man protects his household and his property, so protect Your sanctuary."

[The narrator] said: Then birds came from the sea in flocks (ababil), each bird carrying three stones: two stones in its feet and a stone in its beak. The stones were hurled upon them; they struck nothing without crushing it, except that only that spot [was affected]. That was the first time smallpox, measles and bitter pox were seen, and the stones annihilated them. God sent a violent flood which carried them to the sea and cast them into it. Abraha and those who remained with him fled, and Abraha began to fall apart limb by limb.

As for Mahmud, the elephant of the Negus, it lay down and did not advance on the sacred precinct, so it was saved. As for the other elephant, it advanced and was stoned. It is said there were twelve elephants.

Ibn Ishaq said: When God turned back the Abyssinians from Makkah, the Arabs magnified Quraysh and said: "The People of God; He fought for them and spared them the burden of their enemy." 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar ibn Makhzum said concerning the story of the People of the Elephant:

"You are the Majestic, our Lord, You are not defiled.
You imprisoned the elephant at al-Mughammas,
after they had come, a wretched, despairing folk.
You imprisoned it in the shape of one overturned,
and for them there is no escape nor breath."
Al-mukarkas: the upturned, the cast down. [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 20/196.]]

Abu al-Salt ibn Umayya ibn Mas'ud also said about this:

"Indeed the signs of our Lord are lasting; none disputes concerning them except the disbelievers.
He imprisoned the elephant at al-Mughammas until it crawled about as if it were wounded.
Around it were kings of Kindah [champions], warriors of the battles, falcons.
They left it, then fled swiftly, each one of them with a broken leg bone." [[Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 4/591.]]

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: The commander of the army was Abraha, and Abu Yaksum was one of his viziers and boon companions. When God the Glorified destroyed them with stones, none escaped except Abu Yaksum. He set out, and a bird flew above him without his noticing, until he entered upon the Negus and informed him of what had befallen them. When he finished his speech, the bird struck him and he fell and died, and God showed the Negus how his companions had perished. [[Al-Tabari mentioned it in detail in his tafsir: 1/550–557.]]

Others said: Abu Yaksum was Abraha ibn al-Sabbah. Al-Waqidi said: Abraha was the grandfather of the Negus who was in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

They differed about the date of the Year of the Elephant. Muqatil said: the matter of the Elephant was forty years before the birth of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him). Al-Kalbi and Ubayd ibn Umayr said: it was twenty-three years before the birth of the Prophet (peace be upon him).

It is related that it was in the year in which the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) was born, and most scholars hold this view, as evidenced by what:

Abu Bakr al-Khawarqi informed us, saying: Abu al-'Abbas al-Da'uli informed us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Khaythamah informed us, saying: Ibrahim ibn al-Mundhir al-Jarrahi informed us, saying: 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Thabit informed us, saying: al-Zubayr ibn Musa informed us, from Abu al-Huwayrith, who said: I heard 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan say to Qabath ibn Ushaym al-Kinani al-Laythi: "O Qabath, are you older or the Messenger of God?" He said: "The Messenger of God is older than me, and I am older than him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was born in the Year of the Elephant, and my mother stood me upon the dung of the elephant."

And 'A'ishah said: I saw the elephant's driver and its keeper in Makkah, blind and crippled, begging for food.

Commentary:
"Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?" Muqatil said: there was only one elephant with them. Al-Dahhak said there were eight, but [the singular] was used for the sake of harmony of verse-endings (li-wifaq ru'us al-ay). Or it is said: he attributed them to the greatest elephant, whose name was Mahmud.

"Did He not make their plot go astray?" from their aim of destroying the Ka'bah. It is said: into error and falsehoods. Muqatil said: into loss.

"And He sent against them birds in flocks (ababil)" — numerous and scattered, following one another.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ayzi said: they were groups like approaching camels. Al-A'sha said:

"A path, and a tall palm whose roots are luxuriant, over which are flocks of birds calling (tanʿab)." [[Al-Sihah: 2/608; al-naʿb: the cry of a bird; al-jabbar from palms: what has grown tall.]]

Imru' al-Qays said:

"You see them swift to the summoner, as if they were flocks of birds beneath a heavy cloud."

Another said:

"My mount almost broke from the cries, when the earth flowed with the thoroughbred flocks (al-ababil)." [[Fath al-Qadir: 5/496.]]

They differed about its singular. Al-Farra' said: it has no singular, like al-shamatit, al-abadid and al-sha'arir, none of which is found in singular form. He said: Abu al-Rawasi, who was trustworthy and reliable, claimed that he heard its singular as *ibalah*; and I have heard from the Arabs one who says: "dhaghth 'ala ibalah," meaning abundance upon abundance.

He said: If someone said its singular is *ibalah*, it would be correct, like dinar and dananir. It is said that the surplus that is on the donkey's load or the camel's fodder is called *ibalah*. Al-Kisa'i said: I used to hear the grammarians say: its singular is *ibbul*, like ajjul and ajajil. Muhammad ibn Jarir related from some grammarians that its singular is *abil*; it is said: horses came *ababil* from here and there.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it had snouts like the snouts of birds and paws like the paws of dogs.

'Ikrimah: it had heads like the heads of beasts of prey, not seen before or after that.

Al-Rabi': it had fangs like the fangs of beasts of prey. 'A'ishah said: it was most like swallows (al-khattatif).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr: green birds with yellow beaks. Abu al-Jawza' said: God created them in the air at that time.

"Hurling them with stones" — the common reading is with ta' for the birds; Talhah and Ashhab al-'Uqayli read *yarmihim* with ya', which is the choice of Abu Hanifah, meaning God, as in His saying: "But it was God who threw" [[Surat al-Anfal: 17.]]. It may also refer back to the birds, since they are free of marks of feminine gender.

"Of sijjil" — Ibn Mas'ud said: the bird-related... "and He hurled them with stones; God sent a wind which struck the stones and increased their force, so that no stone fell upon a man's leg without emerging from the other side, and if it fell on his head it came out from his anus."

"And He made them like eaten husk" — like a crop eaten by animals, then their dung passed through it, it dried and its parts scattered; he likened the cutting of their limbs to the scattering of the parts of dung.

Mujahid said: *al-'asf* is the leaves of wheat. Qatadah: it is the chaff. Al-Hasan said: when we were boys in Medina we used to eat barley when it was cut, and it was called *al-'asf*. Sa'id ibn Jubayr: it is the sprouting barley whose leaves are eaten.

Al-Farra': the tips of the crop before it ears and hardens. 'Ikrimah: like a mountain when it is eaten and becomes hollow. Ibn 'Abbas: it is the outer husk that surrounds the wheat grain like a sheath for it.

Al-Mu'arrikh: it is what is cut from the crop, so its tips have fallen. Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is *al-'asf*, *al-'asifah* and *al-jull*. It is said: like a crop whose grain has been eaten and its straw left. Al-Dahhak said: like food that has been eaten.

Meccan. It has ninety-six letters, twenty words, and five verses.

Naqil ibn Raqim informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Shadhah narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Salim ibn Qutaybah narrated to us, from Shu'bah, from 'Asim, from Zirr, from Ubayy, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Fil, God, Mighty and Majestic, will protect him during the days of his life in this world from slander and transformation."

[259] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 10/441.]]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾

The story, and with God is success.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: The account of the companions of the elephant, as related by some scholars, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from others among the scholars of Yemen and elsewhere who met them, is that a king of the Himyar called Zar'ah Dhu Nuwas had become a Jew, and the Himyar united with him in this, except the people of Najran, who were Christians according to the original ruling of the Gospel (Injil). They had a leader called 'Abd Allah ibn al-Tamir. He invited them to Judaism, but they refused, so he gave them a choice, and they chose death. He dug a trench for them and devised for them various kinds of execution.

Some of them were killed by being made to stand as targets, and others he burned in the fire of the trench. But a man from Saba' called Dawas ibn Tha'laban escaped on his horse and galloped until he outran them in the sand. He went to Caesar (Qayṣar) and told him what had befallen them and asked for help. Caesar said: "Your land is far from us, but I will write to the king of Abyssinia, for he is on our religion, and he will support you." So he wrote to the Negus (al-Najashi), ordering him to support him.

When he came to the Negus, the Negus sent with him a man from Abyssinia called Aryat. When he sent him off, he said: "If you enter Yemen, kill a third of its men, destroy a third of its land, and send me a third of its captives." When he entered it, he encountered some resistance in battle, and they scattered away from Dhu Nuwas, and his horse carried him off into the sea, where it struck him, and both of them perished together. That was the last of him. Aryat entered Yemen and acted according to what the Negus had ordered.

Dhu Hadr al-Himyari said, concerning what befell the people of Yemen and their soil:

"My eye, may you have no father, you could not bear it; may God save you, for my spittle has run dry,
At the sound of the singing girls when we were intoxicated, and when we were given to drink the choicest wine,
And drinking wine is no shame for me, if my companion does not reproach me for it,
And Ghumdan, of which I told you, whose sons held it aloft on a cliff's summit,
Its lamps of olive oil shining within it, like the flashes of lightning when it is evening,
Then it became ashes after its splendor, and the flame of fire changed its beauty,
And Dhu Nuwas submitted, having given his all, and warned his people of the narrowness of the strait."

[[The verses in full are in Tafsir al-Tabari: 1/547.]]

He said: Aryat remained in Yemen, and the Negus wrote to him: "Hold your position with your army and those with you." He remained for a time. Then Abraha ibn al-Sabah became angry over a matter concerning Abyssinia, until they split into two factions: one group was with him, and another group was with Abraha. Then they clashed. When some of them drew close to others, Abraha sent to Aryat: "Do not let the Abyssinians fight one another in any way until you meet me. Instead, come out to me, and whichever of us kills the other, the army will join him." So he sent to him: "You have been fair."

Aryat was a large, tall, and handsome man, with his spear in his hand. Abraha was a short man, cautious and fleshy, and he had been devout in Christianity. He had left behind a young man (ghulam) called 'Utudah. When they drew near, Aryat raised his spear and struck Abraha's head with it. It fell upon his forehead, splitting his eye, forehead, nose, and lip, and for this reason he was called al-Ashram (the one with the split nose).

'Utudah charged at Aryat and killed him. The Abyssinians gathered around Abraha, and 'Utudah said: "I am 'Utudah, from behind him. I will strike him, neither father nor mother could match his blow." Abraha said: "There was nothing for you before him, O 'Utudah, nor will there be blood money for him." The Negus heard of what Abraha had done, became angry, and swore that he would not leave Abraha until he dragged him by his forelock and trampled his land. He wrote to Abraha: "You have transgressed against my governor and killed him without my command."

Abraha was an arrogant man. When he heard what the Negus had said, he shaved his head, filled a sack with soil from his land, and wrote to the Negus: "O King, Aryat was only your slave, and I am your slave. We disagreed about your affair, and you know Abyssinia better and govern it better. I had wanted him to withdraw and for me to govern it, but he refused, so I killed him. I have heard what the king swore, and I have shaved my head and sent it to him, and I have sent him a sack of soil from his land so that he may place it under his feet." When that reached him, he was pleased with him and confirmed him in his post, and wrote to him to remain with those of the army who were with him.

Then Abraha built a church in Sana'a called al-Qulays, and he wrote to the Negus: "I have built for you in Sana'a a church the like of which no king has ever built, and I will not stop until I divert to it the pilgrimage of the Arabs." A man from the Banu Malik ibn Kinanah heard of this, so he went out to al-Qulays, entered it at night, and sat there. It was reported to Abraha, and it is said that he came to it looking at it, and Abraha entered and found the filth (al-'adhirah). He said: "Who has dared against me?" It was said: "A man from the Arabs, from the people of that House, did this. He heard what you said and did this." Abraha swore at that moment that he would march to the Ka'bah until he destroyed it.

He set out marching with the Abyssinians, and with him he brought the elephant. The Arabs heard of this, and they were greatly alarmed and found it hideous, and they regarded fighting him as a duty upon them. A king of the Himyar called Dhu Nafar came out with those of his people who obeyed him, and he confronted Abraha, defeated him, and captured Dhu Nafar, bringing him to Abraha. Dhu Nafar said: "O King, do not kill me, for sparing me is better for you than killing me." So he spared him and bound him.

Abraha was a forbearing man. Then he set out marching until he approached the lands of Khath'am. Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami came out with the two tribes of Khath'am, Shahran and Nahs, and those who had gathered to him from the tribes of Yemen. They fought him, and he defeated them and captured Nufayl. Nufayl said: "O King, I am a guide in the land of the Arabs. Do not kill me, and these two hands of mine are pledged for my people to hear and obey." So he spared him and took him along to guide him. When he passed by al-Ta'if, Mas'ud ibn Mu'attib came out to him with men of Thaqif and said: "O King, we are only your slaves, and we have no opposition to you. This house of ours is not the house you seek"—meaning al-Lat—"you seek only the House in Mecca. We will send someone to guide you to it." They sent Abu Righal, their client (mawla), and he went until, when he reached al-Mughammas, Abu Righal died. He is the one whose grave is stoned.

From al-Mughammas, Abraha sent a man from the Habash called al-Aswad ibn Maqsud at the head of his cavalry vanguard. He gathered the wealth of the Sanctuary (haram) and seized two hundred camels belonging to 'Abd al-Muttalib. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar ibn Makhzum said:

"O God, disgrace al-Aswad ibn Maqsud,
the one who seized the large herd, with the marked camels among them,
Between Hira' and Thabir and the desert, detaining them while they are following one after another,
Gather them to the black Tamatim [[the non-Arab foreigners]], who have agreed, or may there be a deity to be worshipped,
And they demolish the sacred House, the honored one, and the two hills of Safa and Marwah and the sacred sites,
Dash him, O Lord, and You are the Praised."

[[Al-hajmah: a large herd of camels. Al-taqlid: marking an animal as an offering. Al-bayd: plural of bayda', a wilderness. Hira' and Thabir: two mountains in Mecca. Tatrid of camels: their following one after another. Al-tamatim: the foreigners.]]

Then Abraha sent Hanatah al-Himyari to the people of Mecca and said: "Ask about its chief, then convey to him what I have sent you with. Tell him that I did not come to fight, but only to demolish this House." He went and entered Mecca, and met 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim and said: "The king has sent me to you to tell you that he has not come to fight unless you fight him, but he has come only to demolish this House, and then he will depart from you."

'Abd al-Muttalib said: "We have no power against him, nor do we have the means to confront him. We will leave him free to do what he came for, for this is the Sacred House of God and the House of His friend Abraham (peace be upon him). If He protects it, it is His House and His sanctuary; and if He leaves it between him and that, by God, we have no strength against it." He said: "Come with me to the king." It is claimed by some scholars that he rode with him on a mule that he had and some of his sons rode with him, until they reached the army.

Dhu Nafar was a friend of 'Abd al-Muttalib, so he came to him and said: "O Dhu Nafar, do you have any help to offer in what has befallen us?"

He said: "What help can a captive man give who cannot be sure he will not be killed morning and evening? But I will send to Unays, the elephant driver, for he is a friend of mine. Ask him to do for you what good he can before the king, and to exalt your rank and standing with him."

He sent for Unays, who came to him, and he said: "This is the chief of Quraysh and the owner of the caravans of Mecca, who feeds people in the plains and the wilderness and on the mountain peaks. The king has seized two hundred camels from him. If you can help him with the king, then do so, for he is my friend, and I love that he should receive whatever good may reach him." Unays entered upon Abraha and said: "O King, this is the chief of Quraysh and the owner of the caravans of Mecca, who feeds people in the plains and the wilderness and on the mountain peaks. He asks permission to see you, and I would like you to permit him so that he may speak with you. He has come not opposing you nor hostile to you, so grant him permission."

'Abd al-Muttalib was a large, tall, and handsome man. When Abraha saw him, he was impressed and honored him, but he disliked that he should sit with him on his throne and that he should sit beneath him. So he came down to the carpet and sat upon it, then he called him and had him sit with him. Then he said to his interpreter: "Tell him: what is your need of the king?" The interpreter said that to him.

'Abd al-Muttalib said: "My need of the king is that he return to me the two hundred camels he has taken from me." Abraha said to his interpreter: "You impressed me when I saw you, but now I have lost respect for you." He said: "Why?" He said: "You came to a House which is your religion and the religion of your fathers, and your protection, to demolish it, and you did not speak to me about it, but you speak to me about two hundred camels that were taken from you?" 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "I am the lord of these camels, and this House has a Lord who will protect it."

He said: "He will not prevent me from it." He said: "Then you and that matter." So he ordered his camels returned to him.

Ibn Ishaq said: It is claimed by some scholars that he went to Abraha with 'Umar ibn Nathah [[So it is in the manuscript; perhaps it is: Layth.]] ibn 'Adi ibn al-Wa'il ibn Bakr ibn 'Abd Manat ibn Kinanah, who at that time was the chief of the Banu Kinanah, and Khuwaylid ibn Wa'ilah al-Hudhali, who at that time was the chief of the Banu Hudhayl. They offered Abraha a third of the wealth of the people of Tihamah on condition that he would turn back from them and not demolish the House, but he refused. When the camels were returned to 'Abd al-Muttalib, he went out and informed Quraysh of the news, and told them to disperse into the ravines and take refuge on the mountain peaks, fearing for them the harm of the army when it entered. They did so. 'Abd al-Muttalib came to the Ka'bah, took hold of the ring of the door, and began to say:

"O Lord, I hope for none but You for them,
O Lord, protect from them Your sanctuary.
Let not their cross or their stratagems overcome Your devotees tomorrow.
They have brought the armies of their lands and the elephant to take Your dependents captive.
They have aimed at Your sanctuary with their scheming, in ignorance, and they have not regarded Your majesty.
If You are leaving them and our Ka'bah, then do as You see fit."

[[Zad al-Masir: 8/310, and Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/554.]]

Then 'Abd al-Muttalib left the ring and went off with his people in some of those directions. Abraha awoke at al-Mughammas, prepared for entry, arranged his army, and readied his elephant. The name of the elephant was Mahmud. It was the elephant of the Negus, which he had sent to Abraha, and it was an elephant the like of which had not been seen on earth in size, body, and strength.

It is said that there were twelve elephants with him. Nufayl came to the largest elephant, took hold of its ear, and said: "Kneel, Mahmud, and return safely from where you came, for you are in the sacred land of God." The elephant knelt, and they tried to make it rise, but it refused. They struck it on the head with the iron hook, but it refused. They put their hooks beneath its belly and its elbows and pulled it to make it stand, but it refused. They turned it back toward Yemen, and it got up and ran; they turned it toward Syria, and it did the same; they turned it toward the east, and it did the same. Then they turned it toward the Sanctuary, and it knelt and refused to rise. It ran off, galloping, until it climbed the mountain.

God sent birds from the sea, like swallows (khatatif), each bird carrying three stones: two stones in its feet, and a stone in its beak, like chickpeas and lentils. When they came over them, it released them upon them, and those stones struck no one without him perishing.

Not all of the people were struck, and they went out fleeing, rushing along the road by which they had come, asking about Nufayl ibn Habib to guide them to the road to Yemen. Nufayl ibn Habib said, when he saw what God had brought down upon them of His vengeance:

"Where is the escape, when the God is the one who seeks?
And the Ashram, the defeated, not the victor?"

[[al-Ashram: he is Abraha, so called because a stone struck him and split his nose.]] [[Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/555.]]

Nufayl also said about that:

"Did not greet us, O Radinah? Yes, you have greeted us, and we have given you our eye with the dawn.
Radinah, if you had seen and had not been seen by the side of al-Muhassab, we would have seen what we saw,
Then you would have excused me, and praised my opinion, and you would not have grieved over what had passed between us.
I praised God when I saw the birds, and I feared stones that would fall upon us.
So all the people ask about Nufayl, as if I owed a debt to the Abyssinians."

[[The same source: 1/555, Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 20/199, and al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah: 2/216.]]

Nufayl was watching them from some of the mountains, while the people were crying out and some were agitating against others. They went out falling along every road and dying at every watering place. A disease fell upon Abraha's body, and his fingertips began to fall off. Every time a fingertip fell, a stream of pus and blood followed it. He reached Sana'a like a young bird, with those of his companions who remained, and he did not die until his chest split open from his heart, and then he perished.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman claimed that the cause that led to the story of the companions of the elephant was that a group from Quraysh went out as merchants to the land of the Negus. They traveled until they approached the seashore, and in one of its sand dunes there was a church of the Christians, which Quraysh called the Haykal, and the Negus and the people of his land called it Atas Hanan. The people knelt to block it, gathered firewood, and lit a fire and cooked. When they departed, they left the fire as it was on a windy day. The winds rushed, and the Haykal burst into flames. The messenger went to the Negus and informed him. At that, he was grieved with anger for the church, so Abraha was sent to demolish the Ka'bah [and what he encountered].

In Mecca at that time was Abu Mas'ud al-Thaqafi, who was blind. He spent summers in al-Ta'if and winters in Mecca. He was an intelligent and noble man who decided matters by his opinion, and he was the first to mend and the first to sever. He was a close friend of 'Abd al-Muttalib. 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "O Abu Mas'ud, what do you have to offer? This is a day in which one cannot do without your opinion."

Abu Mas'ud said to 'Abd al-Muttalib: "Go to a hundred camels and make them a sacred offering to God, mark them with sandals, and then station them in the Sanctuary. Perhaps some of these blacks will slaughter some of them, and the Lord of this House will be angered and seize them." 'Abd al-Muttalib did so. The people went to those camels, attacked them, and slaughtered some of them, and 'Abd al-Muttalib began to supplicate.

Abu Mas'ud said: [and 'Abd al-Muttalib said]: "This House has a Lord who protects it. Tubba', the king of Yemen, came to this rock of the House and wished to demolish it, but God prevented him and afflicted him, and darkness fell upon him for three days. When Tubba' saw that, he clothed the House in white Coptic cloth, honored it, and slaughtered sacrificial camels for it. So look toward the House."

'Abd al-Muttalib looked and said: "I see white birds rising from the seashore." He said: "Watch them with your eyes, and see where they settle." He said: "I see that they have gathered over our heads." He said: "Do you know them?" He said: "By God, I do not know them. They are neither from Najd, nor from Tihamah, nor Arab, nor Syrian, and they are birds in our land that are not familiar."

He said: "What is their shape?" He said: "They are like swallows, with pebbles in their beaks like pebbles of Hadhdh, and they came like locusts, pushing one another, in front of every bird, led by one with a red beak, black head, and long neck. They came until, when they were opposite the army, they settled over their heads."

When all the flocks had gathered, the birds poured what was in their beaks over those beneath them. Written upon each stone was the name of its owner. Then they turned back from where they had come. When morning came, the two of them descended from the peak of the mountain and walked slowly, and they did not see anyone; then they drew near, walking slowly, and heard no sound. They said: "The people spent the night in a stupor and have awakened asleep." When they drew near the army, behold, they were all dead.

A stone would fall upon one of their eggs (or heads), piercing it until it reached the brain, and would pierce the elephant and the animal, and the stone would sink into the earth from the force of its impact. 'Abd al-Muttalib then took one of their axes and dug until he reached deep into the earth, and filled it with red gold and fine jewels. He dug for his companion and filled it, and then said to Abu Mas'ud: "Bring your ring and choose. If you want, you may take my pit, if you want, you may take yours, and if you want, both of them are yours together."

Then Ibn Mas'ud said: "You chose me over yourself." 'Abd al-Muttalib replied: "I have not failed to place the finest of goods in my pit, so it is yours." Each of them sat by his pit, and 'Abd al-Muttalib called out to the people, so they returned and took from their surplus until they could no longer bear it. 'Abd al-Muttalib thereby became the leader of Quraysh, and they granted him the leadership. 'Abd al-Muttalib and Abu Mas'ud remained, with their families, in wealth from that money. God repelled [the enemy] from His Ka'bah and His qiblah, sending against them hosts they had no power to withstand.

Al-Waqidi said, with his chains of narration: Abraha sent Aryat, Abu Dukhma, with four thousand [men] to Yemen. He overcame it, honored the kings and humiliated the poor. Then a man from Abyssinia called Abraha al-Ashram, Abu Yaksum, rose up and called for obedience to himself, and they answered him. He killed Aryat and overcame Yemen. He saw people preparing for the Hajj and said: "Where are the people going?" He was told: "They are making pilgrimage to the House of God in Makkah." He said: "What is it made of?" He was told: "Of stones." He said: "What is its covering?" He was told: "What comes from here and there."

He said: "By the Messiah, I will build for them something better than it." So he built for them a house, constructed of white, red, yellow and black marble, adorned it with gold and silver, surrounded it with jewels, placed in it a great red ruby, appointed chamberlains for it, burned aloes wood (al-mandali) in it, and smeared its walls with musk, so that they blackened, until the jewels were hidden. He ordered the people to make pilgrimage to it, and many tribes of the Arabs made pilgrimage to it for years. Men remained in it worshipping and devoting themselves to it, and they performed rites for it.

Nufayl al-Khath'ami used to annoy him with what he disliked, so he was given respite. Then one night he saw no one moving, so he went, brought excrement, smeared it on its forehead, gathered carrion and threw it into it. Abraha was informed of this and became extremely angry, and said: "The Arabs have only acted out of zeal for their house. I will surely demolish it stone by stone." He wrote to the Negus informing him of this and asking him to send him his elephant Mahmud, an elephant unmatched on earth in size, body and strength, and he sent it to him.

When the elephant reached him, Abraha marched with the people, accompanied by the king of Himyar and Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami. When he approached the sacred precinct (al-haram), he ordered his companions to raid the people's camels, and they seized camels belonging to 'Abd al-Muttalib. Nufayl was a friend of 'Abd al-Muttalib, so he spoke to Abraha about his camels. Nufayl spoke to Abraha, saying: "O King, the chief of the Arabs, the most excellent of them in rank and the most ancient in nobility, has come to you; he carries [people] on thoroughbred horses, gives wealth, and feeds the people." So he was brought in to Abraha, who said: "What is your need?" He said: "That you return my camels to me." Abraha said: "I did not think, from what has reached me of you, except [that you would be] deceptive; I had thought you would speak to me about your House, which is your honor." 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "Return my camels to me, and as for the House, it has a Lord who will protect it."

So he ordered his camels returned to him. When he took them, he hung sandals on them, marked them, made them offerings, and let them loose in the sacred precinct so that some of them would be struck, and the Lord of the sacred precinct would be angered. 'Abd al-Muttalib went out on horses, accompanied by 'Amr ibn 'Abid ibn 'Imran ibn Makhzum ibn Mut'im ibn 'Adi, and Abu Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "O God, a man protects his household and his property, so protect Your sanctuary."

[The narrator] said: Then birds came from the sea in flocks (ababil), each bird carrying three stones: two stones in its feet and a stone in its beak. The stones were hurled upon them; they struck nothing without crushing it, except that only that spot [was affected]. That was the first time smallpox, measles and bitter pox were seen, and the stones annihilated them. God sent a violent flood which carried them to the sea and cast them into it. Abraha and those who remained with him fled, and Abraha began to fall apart limb by limb.

As for Mahmud, the elephant of the Negus, it lay down and did not advance on the sacred precinct, so it was saved. As for the other elephant, it advanced and was stoned. It is said there were twelve elephants.

Ibn Ishaq said: When God turned back the Abyssinians from Makkah, the Arabs magnified Quraysh and said: "The People of God; He fought for them and spared them the burden of their enemy." 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar ibn Makhzum said concerning the story of the People of the Elephant:

"You are the Majestic, our Lord, You are not defiled.
You imprisoned the elephant at al-Mughammas,
after they had come, a wretched, despairing folk.
You imprisoned it in the shape of one overturned,
and for them there is no escape nor breath."
Al-mukarkas: the upturned, the cast down. [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 20/196.]]

Abu al-Salt ibn Umayya ibn Mas'ud also said about this:

"Indeed the signs of our Lord are lasting; none disputes concerning them except the disbelievers.
He imprisoned the elephant at al-Mughammas until it crawled about as if it were wounded.
Around it were kings of Kindah [champions], warriors of the battles, falcons.
They left it, then fled swiftly, each one of them with a broken leg bone." [[Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 4/591.]]

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: The commander of the army was Abraha, and Abu Yaksum was one of his viziers and boon companions. When God the Glorified destroyed them with stones, none escaped except Abu Yaksum. He set out, and a bird flew above him without his noticing, until he entered upon the Negus and informed him of what had befallen them. When he finished his speech, the bird struck him and he fell and died, and God showed the Negus how his companions had perished. [[Al-Tabari mentioned it in detail in his tafsir: 1/550–557.]]

Others said: Abu Yaksum was Abraha ibn al-Sabbah. Al-Waqidi said: Abraha was the grandfather of the Negus who was in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

They differed about the date of the Year of the Elephant. Muqatil said: the matter of the Elephant was forty years before the birth of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him). Al-Kalbi and Ubayd ibn Umayr said: it was twenty-three years before the birth of the Prophet (peace be upon him).

It is related that it was in the year in which the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) was born, and most scholars hold this view, as evidenced by what:

Abu Bakr al-Khawarqi informed us, saying: Abu al-'Abbas al-Da'uli informed us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Khaythamah informed us, saying: Ibrahim ibn al-Mundhir al-Jarrahi informed us, saying: 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Thabit informed us, saying: al-Zubayr ibn Musa informed us, from Abu al-Huwayrith, who said: I heard 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan say to Qabath ibn Ushaym al-Kinani al-Laythi: "O Qabath, are you older or the Messenger of God?" He said: "The Messenger of God is older than me, and I am older than him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was born in the Year of the Elephant, and my mother stood me upon the dung of the elephant."

And 'A'ishah said: I saw the elephant's driver and its keeper in Makkah, blind and crippled, begging for food.

Commentary:
"Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?" Muqatil said: there was only one elephant with them. Al-Dahhak said there were eight, but [the singular] was used for the sake of harmony of verse-endings (li-wifaq ru'us al-ay). Or it is said: he attributed them to the greatest elephant, whose name was Mahmud.

"Did He not make their plot go astray?" from their aim of destroying the Ka'bah. It is said: into error and falsehoods. Muqatil said: into loss.

"And He sent against them birds in flocks (ababil)" — numerous and scattered, following one another.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ayzi said: they were groups like approaching camels. Al-A'sha said:

"A path, and a tall palm whose roots are luxuriant, over which are flocks of birds calling (tanʿab)." [[Al-Sihah: 2/608; al-naʿb: the cry of a bird; al-jabbar from palms: what has grown tall.]]

Imru' al-Qays said:

"You see them swift to the summoner, as if they were flocks of birds beneath a heavy cloud."

Another said:

"My mount almost broke from the cries, when the earth flowed with the thoroughbred flocks (al-ababil)." [[Fath al-Qadir: 5/496.]]

They differed about its singular. Al-Farra' said: it has no singular, like al-shamatit, al-abadid and al-sha'arir, none of which is found in singular form. He said: Abu al-Rawasi, who was trustworthy and reliable, claimed that he heard its singular as *ibalah*; and I have heard from the Arabs one who says: "dhaghth 'ala ibalah," meaning abundance upon abundance.

He said: If someone said its singular is *ibalah*, it would be correct, like dinar and dananir. It is said that the surplus that is on the donkey's load or the camel's fodder is called *ibalah*. Al-Kisa'i said: I used to hear the grammarians say: its singular is *ibbul*, like ajjul and ajajil. Muhammad ibn Jarir related from some grammarians that its singular is *abil*; it is said: horses came *ababil* from here and there.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it had snouts like the snouts of birds and paws like the paws of dogs.

'Ikrimah: it had heads like the heads of beasts of prey, not seen before or after that.

Al-Rabi': it had fangs like the fangs of beasts of prey. 'A'ishah said: it was most like swallows (al-khattatif).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr: green birds with yellow beaks. Abu al-Jawza' said: God created them in the air at that time.

"Hurling them with stones" — the common reading is with ta' for the birds; Talhah and Ashhab al-'Uqayli read *yarmihim* with ya', which is the choice of Abu Hanifah, meaning God, as in His saying: "But it was God who threw" [[Surat al-Anfal: 17.]]. It may also refer back to the birds, since they are free of marks of feminine gender.

"Of sijjil" — Ibn Mas'ud said: the bird-related... "and He hurled them with stones; God sent a wind which struck the stones and increased their force, so that no stone fell upon a man's leg without emerging from the other side, and if it fell on his head it came out from his anus."

"And He made them like eaten husk" — like a crop eaten by animals, then their dung passed through it, it dried and its parts scattered; he likened the cutting of their limbs to the scattering of the parts of dung.

Mujahid said: *al-'asf* is the leaves of wheat. Qatadah: it is the chaff. Al-Hasan said: when we were boys in Medina we used to eat barley when it was cut, and it was called *al-'asf*. Sa'id ibn Jubayr: it is the sprouting barley whose leaves are eaten.

Al-Farra': the tips of the crop before it ears and hardens. 'Ikrimah: like a mountain when it is eaten and becomes hollow. Ibn 'Abbas: it is the outer husk that surrounds the wheat grain like a sheath for it.

Al-Mu'arrikh: it is what is cut from the crop, so its tips have fallen. Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is *al-'asf*, *al-'asifah* and *al-jull*. It is said: like a crop whose grain has been eaten and its straw left. Al-Dahhak said: like food that has been eaten.

Meccan. It has ninety-six letters, twenty words, and five verses.

Naqil ibn Raqim informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Shadhah narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Salim ibn Qutaybah narrated to us, from Shu'bah, from 'Asim, from Zirr, from Ubayy, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Fil, God, Mighty and Majestic, will protect him during the days of his life in this world from slander and transformation."

[259] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 10/441.]]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾

The story, and with God is success.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: The account of the companions of the elephant, as related by some scholars, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from others among the scholars of Yemen and elsewhere who met them, is that a king of the Himyar called Zar'ah Dhu Nuwas had become a Jew, and the Himyar united with him in this, except the people of Najran, who were Christians according to the original ruling of the Gospel (Injil). They had a leader called 'Abd Allah ibn al-Tamir. He invited them to Judaism, but they refused, so he gave them a choice, and they chose death. He dug a trench for them and devised for them various kinds of execution.

Some of them were killed by being made to stand as targets, and others he burned in the fire of the trench. But a man from Saba' called Dawas ibn Tha'laban escaped on his horse and galloped until he outran them in the sand. He went to Caesar (Qayṣar) and told him what had befallen them and asked for help. Caesar said: "Your land is far from us, but I will write to the king of Abyssinia, for he is on our religion, and he will support you." So he wrote to the Negus (al-Najashi), ordering him to support him.

When he came to the Negus, the Negus sent with him a man from Abyssinia called Aryat. When he sent him off, he said: "If you enter Yemen, kill a third of its men, destroy a third of its land, and send me a third of its captives." When he entered it, he encountered some resistance in battle, and they scattered away from Dhu Nuwas, and his horse carried him off into the sea, where it struck him, and both of them perished together. That was the last of him. Aryat entered Yemen and acted according to what the Negus had ordered.

Dhu Hadr al-Himyari said, concerning what befell the people of Yemen and their soil:

"My eye, may you have no father, you could not bear it; may God save you, for my spittle has run dry,
At the sound of the singing girls when we were intoxicated, and when we were given to drink the choicest wine,
And drinking wine is no shame for me, if my companion does not reproach me for it,
And Ghumdan, of which I told you, whose sons held it aloft on a cliff's summit,
Its lamps of olive oil shining within it, like the flashes of lightning when it is evening,
Then it became ashes after its splendor, and the flame of fire changed its beauty,
And Dhu Nuwas submitted, having given his all, and warned his people of the narrowness of the strait."

[[The verses in full are in Tafsir al-Tabari: 1/547.]]

He said: Aryat remained in Yemen, and the Negus wrote to him: "Hold your position with your army and those with you." He remained for a time. Then Abraha ibn al-Sabah became angry over a matter concerning Abyssinia, until they split into two factions: one group was with him, and another group was with Abraha. Then they clashed. When some of them drew close to others, Abraha sent to Aryat: "Do not let the Abyssinians fight one another in any way until you meet me. Instead, come out to me, and whichever of us kills the other, the army will join him." So he sent to him: "You have been fair."

Aryat was a large, tall, and handsome man, with his spear in his hand. Abraha was a short man, cautious and fleshy, and he had been devout in Christianity. He had left behind a young man (ghulam) called 'Utudah. When they drew near, Aryat raised his spear and struck Abraha's head with it. It fell upon his forehead, splitting his eye, forehead, nose, and lip, and for this reason he was called al-Ashram (the one with the split nose).

'Utudah charged at Aryat and killed him. The Abyssinians gathered around Abraha, and 'Utudah said: "I am 'Utudah, from behind him. I will strike him, neither father nor mother could match his blow." Abraha said: "There was nothing for you before him, O 'Utudah, nor will there be blood money for him." The Negus heard of what Abraha had done, became angry, and swore that he would not leave Abraha until he dragged him by his forelock and trampled his land. He wrote to Abraha: "You have transgressed against my governor and killed him without my command."

Abraha was an arrogant man. When he heard what the Negus had said, he shaved his head, filled a sack with soil from his land, and wrote to the Negus: "O King, Aryat was only your slave, and I am your slave. We disagreed about your affair, and you know Abyssinia better and govern it better. I had wanted him to withdraw and for me to govern it, but he refused, so I killed him. I have heard what the king swore, and I have shaved my head and sent it to him, and I have sent him a sack of soil from his land so that he may place it under his feet." When that reached him, he was pleased with him and confirmed him in his post, and wrote to him to remain with those of the army who were with him.

Then Abraha built a church in Sana'a called al-Qulays, and he wrote to the Negus: "I have built for you in Sana'a a church the like of which no king has ever built, and I will not stop until I divert to it the pilgrimage of the Arabs." A man from the Banu Malik ibn Kinanah heard of this, so he went out to al-Qulays, entered it at night, and sat there. It was reported to Abraha, and it is said that he came to it looking at it, and Abraha entered and found the filth (al-'adhirah). He said: "Who has dared against me?" It was said: "A man from the Arabs, from the people of that House, did this. He heard what you said and did this." Abraha swore at that moment that he would march to the Ka'bah until he destroyed it.

He set out marching with the Abyssinians, and with him he brought the elephant. The Arabs heard of this, and they were greatly alarmed and found it hideous, and they regarded fighting him as a duty upon them. A king of the Himyar called Dhu Nafar came out with those of his people who obeyed him, and he confronted Abraha, defeated him, and captured Dhu Nafar, bringing him to Abraha. Dhu Nafar said: "O King, do not kill me, for sparing me is better for you than killing me." So he spared him and bound him.

Abraha was a forbearing man. Then he set out marching until he approached the lands of Khath'am. Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami came out with the two tribes of Khath'am, Shahran and Nahs, and those who had gathered to him from the tribes of Yemen. They fought him, and he defeated them and captured Nufayl. Nufayl said: "O King, I am a guide in the land of the Arabs. Do not kill me, and these two hands of mine are pledged for my people to hear and obey." So he spared him and took him along to guide him. When he passed by al-Ta'if, Mas'ud ibn Mu'attib came out to him with men of Thaqif and said: "O King, we are only your slaves, and we have no opposition to you. This house of ours is not the house you seek"—meaning al-Lat—"you seek only the House in Mecca. We will send someone to guide you to it." They sent Abu Righal, their client (mawla), and he went until, when he reached al-Mughammas, Abu Righal died. He is the one whose grave is stoned.

From al-Mughammas, Abraha sent a man from the Habash called al-Aswad ibn Maqsud at the head of his cavalry vanguard. He gathered the wealth of the Sanctuary (haram) and seized two hundred camels belonging to 'Abd al-Muttalib. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar ibn Makhzum said:

"O God, disgrace al-Aswad ibn Maqsud,
the one who seized the large herd, with the marked camels among them,
Between Hira' and Thabir and the desert, detaining them while they are following one after another,
Gather them to the black Tamatim [[the non-Arab foreigners]], who have agreed, or may there be a deity to be worshipped,
And they demolish the sacred House, the honored one, and the two hills of Safa and Marwah and the sacred sites,
Dash him, O Lord, and You are the Praised."

[[Al-hajmah: a large herd of camels. Al-taqlid: marking an animal as an offering. Al-bayd: plural of bayda', a wilderness. Hira' and Thabir: two mountains in Mecca. Tatrid of camels: their following one after another. Al-tamatim: the foreigners.]]

Then Abraha sent Hanatah al-Himyari to the people of Mecca and said: "Ask about its chief, then convey to him what I have sent you with. Tell him that I did not come to fight, but only to demolish this House." He went and entered Mecca, and met 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim and said: "The king has sent me to you to tell you that he has not come to fight unless you fight him, but he has come only to demolish this House, and then he will depart from you."

'Abd al-Muttalib said: "We have no power against him, nor do we have the means to confront him. We will leave him free to do what he came for, for this is the Sacred House of God and the House of His friend Abraham (peace be upon him). If He protects it, it is His House and His sanctuary; and if He leaves it between him and that, by God, we have no strength against it." He said: "Come with me to the king." It is claimed by some scholars that he rode with him on a mule that he had and some of his sons rode with him, until they reached the army.

Dhu Nafar was a friend of 'Abd al-Muttalib, so he came to him and said: "O Dhu Nafar, do you have any help to offer in what has befallen us?"

He said: "What help can a captive man give who cannot be sure he will not be killed morning and evening? But I will send to Unays, the elephant driver, for he is a friend of mine. Ask him to do for you what good he can before the king, and to exalt your rank and standing with him."

He sent for Unays, who came to him, and he said: "This is the chief of Quraysh and the owner of the caravans of Mecca, who feeds people in the plains and the wilderness and on the mountain peaks. The king has seized two hundred camels from him. If you can help him with the king, then do so, for he is my friend, and I love that he should receive whatever good may reach him." Unays entered upon Abraha and said: "O King, this is the chief of Quraysh and the owner of the caravans of Mecca, who feeds people in the plains and the wilderness and on the mountain peaks. He asks permission to see you, and I would like you to permit him so that he may speak with you. He has come not opposing you nor hostile to you, so grant him permission."

'Abd al-Muttalib was a large, tall, and handsome man. When Abraha saw him, he was impressed and honored him, but he disliked that he should sit with him on his throne and that he should sit beneath him. So he came down to the carpet and sat upon it, then he called him and had him sit with him. Then he said to his interpreter: "Tell him: what is your need of the king?" The interpreter said that to him.

'Abd al-Muttalib said: "My need of the king is that he return to me the two hundred camels he has taken from me." Abraha said to his interpreter: "You impressed me when I saw you, but now I have lost respect for you." He said: "Why?" He said: "You came to a House which is your religion and the religion of your fathers, and your protection, to demolish it, and you did not speak to me about it, but you speak to me about two hundred camels that were taken from you?" 'Abd al-Muttalib said: "I am the lord of these camels, and this House has a Lord who will protect it."

He said: "He will not prevent me from it." He said: "Then you and that matter." So he ordered his camels returned to him.

Ibn Ishaq said: It is claimed by some scholars that he went to Abraha with 'Umar ibn Nathah [[So it is in the manuscript; perhaps it is: Layth.]] ibn 'Adi ibn al-Wa'il ibn Bakr ibn 'Abd Manat ibn Kinanah, who at that time was the chief of the Banu Kinanah, and Khuwaylid ibn Wa'ilah al-Hudhali, who at that time was the chief of the Banu Hudhayl. They offered Abraha a third of the wealth of the people of Tihamah on condition that he would turn back from them and not demolish the House, but he refused. When the camels were returned to 'Abd al-Muttalib, he went out and informed Quraysh of the news, and told them to disperse into the ravines and take refuge on the mountain peaks, fearing for them the harm of the army when it entered. They did so. 'Abd al-Muttalib came to the Ka'bah, took hold of the ring of the door, and began to say:

"O Lord, I hope for none but You for them,
O Lord, protect from them Your sanctuary.
Let not their cross or their stratagems overcome Your devotees tomorrow.
They have brought the armies of their lands and the elephant to take Your dependents captive.
They have aimed at Your sanctuary with their scheming, in ignorance, and they have not regarded Your majesty.
If You are leaving them and our Ka'bah, then do as You see fit."

[[Zad al-Masir: 8/310, and Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/554.]]

Then 'Abd al-Muttalib left the ring and went off with his people in some of those directions. Abraha awoke at al-Mughammas, prepared for entry, arranged his army, and readied his elephant. The name of the elephant was Mahmud. It was the elephant of the Negus, which he had sent to Abraha, and it was an elephant the like of which had not been seen on earth in size, body, and strength.

It is said that there were twelve elephants with him. Nufayl came to the largest elephant, took hold of its ear, and said: "Kneel, Mahmud, and return safely from where you came, for you are in the sacred land of God." The elephant knelt, and they tried to make it rise, but it refused. They struck it on the head with the iron hook, but it refused. They put their hooks beneath its belly and its elbows and pulled it to make it stand, but it refused. They turned it back toward Yemen, and it got up and ran; they turned it toward Syria, and it did the same; they turned it toward the east, and it did the same. Then they turned it toward the Sanctuary, and it knelt and refused to rise. It ran off, galloping, until it climbed the mountain.

God sent birds from the sea, like swallows (khatatif), each bird carrying three stones: two stones in its feet, and a stone in its beak, like chickpeas and lentils. When they came over them, it released them upon them, and those stones struck no one without him perishing.

Not all of the people were struck, and they went out fleeing, rushing along the road by which they had come, asking about Nufayl ibn Habib to guide them to the road to Yemen. Nufayl ibn Habib said, when he saw what God had brought down upon them of His vengeance:

"Where is the escape, when the God is the one who seeks?
And the Ashram, the defeated, not the victor?"

[[al-Ashram: he is Abraha, so called because a stone struck him and split his nose.]] [[Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/555.]]

Nufayl also said about that:

"Did not greet us, O Radinah? Yes, you have greeted us, and we have given you our eye with the dawn.
Radinah, if you had seen and had not been seen by the side of al-Muhassab, we would have seen what we saw,
Then you would have excused me, and praised my opinion, and you would not have grieved over what had passed between us.
I praised God when I saw the birds, and I feared stones that would fall upon us.
So all the people ask about Nufayl, as if I owed a debt to the Abyssinians."

[[The same source: 1/555, Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 20/199, and al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah: 2/216.]]

Nufayl was watching them from some of the mountains, while the people were crying out and some were agitating against others. They went out falling along every road and dying at every watering place. A disease fell upon Abraha's body, and his fingertips began to fall off. Every time a fingertip fell, a stream of pus and blood followed it. He reached Sana'a like a young bird, with those of his companions who remained, and he did not die until his chest split open from his heart, and then he perished.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman claimed that the cause that led to the story of the companions of the elephant was that a group from Quraysh went out as merchants to the land of the Negus. They traveled until they approached the seashore, and in one of its sand dunes there was a church of the Christians, which Quraysh called the Haykal, and the Negus and the people of his land called it Atas Hanan.
